source_text: Incipiamus igitur probare nativitatem Christi a prophetis esse nuntiatam. Sic Esaias dicit: Audite, domus David, non pusillum vobis certamen cum hominibus, quoniam Deus praestat certamen: propter hoc ipse Deus dabit vobis signum: Ecce virgo concipiet in utero et pariet filium, et vocabitis nomen ejus Emmanuel, quod interpretatur: Nobiscum Deus. Butyrum et mel manducabit. Quoniam, priusquam cognoscat infans vocare patrem aut matrem, accipiet virtutem Damasci, et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum.. Itaque dicunt Judaei: Provocemus istam praedicationem Esaiae, et faciamus comparationem, an Christo qui jam venit, competat illi primo nomen quod Esaias praedicavit, et insignia ejus quae de eo nuntiavit. Equidem Esaias praedicat eum Emmanuelem vocari oportere, dehinc virtutem sumpturum Damasci et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum. Porro, inquiunt, iste qui venit, neque sub ejusmodi nomine est editus, neque re bellica functus. At nos e contrario admonendos eos existimavimus, uti cohaerentia quoque hujus capituli recognoscant: subjuncta est enim et interpretatio Emmanuel, Nobiscum Deus, uti non solum sonum nominis spectes, sed et sensum. Sonus enim hebraicus, quod est Emmanuel, suae gentis est; sensus autem ejus, quod est Deus nobiscum, ex interpretatione communis est. Quaero ergo an ista vox, Nobiscum Deus, quod est Emmanuel, exinde quo Christus inluxit, agitetur in Christo? Et puto, ex toto non negabis. Nam qui ex Judaismo credunt Christo, ex quo in eum credunt, Emmanuel cum volent dicere, nobiscum Deum esse significant. Atque ita constat jam venisse illum qui praedicabatur Emmanuel, quia quod significat Emmanuel, venit, id est Nobiscum Deus. Aeque et sono nominis inducuntur, cum virtutem Damasci, et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum, sic accipiunt, quasi bellatorem portendant Christum, non animadvertentes quid Scriptura praemittat: Quoniam priusquam cognoscat puer vocare patrem aut matrem, accipiet virtutem Damasci et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum. Ante est enim inspicias aetatis demonstrationem, an virum jam Christum exhibere ista aetas possit, nedum imperatorem; scilicet vagitu ad arma esset convocaturus infans; et signum belli, non tuba, sed crepitacillo daturus; nec ex equo vel de muro, sed de nutricis et gerulae suae dorso sive collo hostem destinaturus; atque ita Damascum et Samariam pro mammis subacturus. Aliud est, si penes vos infantes in praelium erumpunt, credo ad solem uncti prius, dehinc pannis armati, et butyro stipendiati, qui ante norint lanceare quam lancinare.
pass_a_gloss: Let us therefore begin to prove that the birth of Christ was announced by the prophets. Thus Isaiah says: Hear, house of David, you have no small contest with men, for God provides the contest: for this reason God Himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and will bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted: God with us. He will eat butter and honey. For, before the infant knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus, and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. Therefore, the Jews say: Let us challenge this prophecy of Isaiah, and let us make a comparison, whether the first name that Isaiah prophesied belongs to Christ who has already come, and the signs that he announced about him. Indeed, Isaiah prophesies that he ought to be called Emmanuel, and then he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. Furthermore, they say, this one who has come, neither was he brought forth under such a name, nor did he engage in war. But we, on the contrary, think that they should be warned, so that they may also recognize the coherence of this chapter: for the interpretation of Emmanuel, God with us, is also added, so that you may consider not only the sound of the name, but also its meaning. For the sound of the Hebrew name Emmanuel is of his own people, but its meaning, which is God with us, is common from the interpretation. I ask, therefore, whether this phrase, God with us, which is Emmanuel, is at work in Christ from the time he shone forth. And I think you will not deny it entirely. For those who believe in Christ from Judaism, from the time they believe in him, when they want to say Emmanuel, they mean that God is with us. And so it is established that he who was prophesied as Emmanuel has already come, because what Emmanuel signifies has come, that is, God with us. Similarly, they are also led by the sound of the name, when they take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians, as if they were portraying Christ as a warrior, not noticing what the Scripture premises: For before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. For first, one must consider the demonstration of age, whether this age can already show Christ as a man, let alone an emperor; certainly, the infant would be summoned to arms with crying, and the sign of war would be given not with a trumpet, but with a rattle; nor would he direct the enemy from a horse or a wall, but from the back or neck of his nurse or carrier; and thus he would subdue Damascus and Samaria for his milk teeth. It is different if, among you, infants burst into battle, I believe they are first anointed with the sun, then armed with swaddling clothes, and paid with butter, who know how to wield a lance before they know how to tear.

pass_b_english: Let us begin, then, by proving that Christ's birth was announced by the prophets. Isaiah says: 'Hear, house of David, you have no small contest with men, for God provides the contest. For this reason God Himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel,' which means 'God with us' (Isaiah 7:14). 'He will eat butter and honey' (Isaiah 7:15). 'For before the infant knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians' (Isaiah 7:16).

So the Jews say: 'Let us challenge this prophecy of Isaiah and make a comparison—whether the first name Isaiah prophesied, and the signs he announced about him, fit the Christ who has already come.' Isaiah does prophesy that he must be called Emmanuel, and then that he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. 'But,' they object, 'this one who came was neither born under such a name nor did he engage in war.' We, on the other hand, think they need a warning to recognize the coherence of this chapter as well: the interpretation 'Emmanuel, God with us' is added so you consider not just the sound of the name, but its meaning. The Hebrew sound 'Emmanuel' belongs to his own people, but its meaning—'God with us'—is common property through translation.

I ask, then, whether this phrase 'God with us,' which is Emmanuel, is operative in Christ from the moment he shone forth. And I think you will not deny it entirely. For those who believe in Christ from Judaism, from the moment they believe in him, when they want to say 'Emmanuel,' they mean that God is with us. And so it stands established that the one prophesied as Emmanuel has already come, because what Emmanuel signifies has come—that is, God with us.

They are likewise misled by the sound of the name when they take 'the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians' as if they were portraying Christ as a warrior, not noticing what the Scripture premises: 'For before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians.' First you must consider the proof of age—whether this age can even present Christ as a man, let alone an emperor. The infant would be summoned to arms by crying; the signal for war would be given not by a trumpet but by a rattle; he would not direct the enemy from a horse or a wall, but from the back or neck of his nurse or carrier; and so he would subdue Damascus and Samaria for his milk teeth. It would be different if infants burst into battle among you—I suppose they are first anointed by the sun, then armed with swaddling clothes, and paid with butter, since they know how to wield a lance before they know how to tear.
